https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly objects to the takedown requests targeting its X handle and posts documenting instances of online censorship in India. 
 
On 3 November 2026 at 3:18 AM and 4:33 AM, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 received an email from X’s Legal Department informing us that it had received takedown requests from the Delhi Police concerning 42 URLs. These include the handles of https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, @internetfreedom, @geoblockedindia, and posts from the said organisations and other users. A separate notification identified five (5) URLs concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X account and our posts.

The requests relate to posts discussing legal notices received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). They also include posts by users who commented on or reshared these posts, as well as other posts by @geoblockedindia documenting instances of digital censorship.

Chain of Events

1. On 29 October 2026, when https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF and @geoblockedindia (collectively “Organisations”) received a legal notice from an advocate purportedly acting on behalf of the RSS. The notice took objection to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's Free Speech Tracker, which documents instances of censorship and online content restrictions and account takedowns in India. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and IFF raised concerns about the authenticity of the notice, which did not carry an official letterhead or identify an authorised signatory.

2. On 1 November 2026, the Organisations received another notice from the same advocate. This notice stated that the matter had been transferred to the RSS's legal and advocacy wing, the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, and referred to complaints allegedly filed in different states.

3. On the same day, X informed https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 that it had received a request from the “Indian Police” alleging that a post discussing the legal notice violated Indian law. However, this notification did not identify the requesting law enforcement agency, statutory provisions invoked, or provide a copy of the underlying order or request. The post remains accessible on X at the time of writing.

4. On 3 November 2026, X communicated further directions from Delhi Police covering 42 URLs, including the URL for https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s account itself. In the attached notices, the first notice refers to Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 which deals with the offence of criminal defamation as the legal basis. The second notice refers to Section 356 of BNS and Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology Rules 2021, which deal with intermediary liability and due diligence of intermediaries as the legal basis. The grounds cited for the takedown requests concerning https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s X handle and posts include hate speech, defamation of RSS, and safety/security.

Takedown requests targeting https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's handle threaten its public service work

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's X handle is an important public-facing channel through which it disseminates the organisation's ongoing work to the general public. It is through https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 social media handles that users who face digital rights violation and online harms reach out to us for pro bono legal services. Through the handle we publish legal and policy analysis, document instances of censorship, raise awareness about digital rights violations, and communicate such information with the public including journalists, researchers, civil society organisations among others. It also serves as a channel for sharing developments concerning internet shutdowns, content restrictions, account takedowns and other violations of digital rights and for providing important assistance, through RightsLine, to citizens facing online harms ranging from gender based violence and harassment  to cyberfraud. 

A direction seeking the takedown of an organisation’s entire account, rather than addressing specific content through a transparent and legally established process, would have consequences far beyond the posts that have been identified. It would also deprive the public of an established and credible source of information on digital rights and the exercise of fundamental freedoms online.

The request to restrict https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s entire X handle, rather than identifying and seeking the removal of specific allegedly unlawful content does not meet the necessity and proportionality standards. The right to freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution extends to disseminate information, circulate ideas and reach an audience.  Restrictions on fundamental freedoms must not be arbitrary or excessive and must not go beyond what is necessary to achieve their legitimate objective (Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1951 SC 118). Any restriction on an organisation's established channel of communication must therefore be assessed in light of its wider impact on the organisation's ability to exercise its rights and the public's corresponding right to receive information.

Further, the reliance on Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, raises questions to whether intermediary liability provisions are being used as an independent mechanism for restricting online speech, potentially bypassing the procedural safeguards prescribed under Section 69A of the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b), clarifying that an intermediary's obligation to remove or disable access to content must arise from a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency, and that such orders or notifications must strictly conform to the grounds enumerated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Section 79(3)(b), which forms part of the intermediary safe-harbour framework, cannot be treated as an unrestricted or independent source of blocking power or used to circumvent the safeguards governing restrictions on online information.

It is also pertinent to note that https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors, W.P.(C) 7650/2025 has also challenged the constitutional legality of the notification issued by Lieutenant Governor (LG) which empowers the Delhi Police to issue takedown orders for removal of online content from social media. The matter is currently pending in the Delhi High Court.

Documenting censorship is not facilitating circumvention

The Free Speech Tracker is an initiative to document instances of censorship in India. Its purpose is to make censorship visible, identify patterns in content moderation and provide the public with information about restrictions affecting online expression.

Documenting a restriction does not amount to endorsing the restricted content, facilitating access to it or encouraging circumvention of the law. Over the last few months, we have seen an unprecedented number of online content restrictions happening in India, and in the absence of adequate transparency from the government and platforms about the nature, extent and legal basis of these restrictions, we wanted to document these instances in a manner that is informative to the general public. Freedom of expression encompasses not only the right to publish and disseminate information but also the right to question restrictions on speech, seek accountability and scrutinise decisions affecting public discourse.

Independent civil society organisations like ours play an important role in documenting these developments and ensuring that restrictions on online expression do not go unnoticed. Such takedown requests risk creating a chilling effect on public-interest advocacy and may discourage individuals from discussing or questioning instances of censorship.

Irregularities in notice received

The first notice received by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 from X, pertains to this post. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of ‘safety/security; defamation; and other’. Furthermore, the notice states that the post is “defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under the Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).” Criminal defamation under Section 356 of the BNS, 2023, is a non-cognizable offence and therefore, requires a court order for the police to initiate action.

The second notice received, pertains to a list of 42 posts and accounts. The notice states that the content in question is being reported on the grounds of “Hate speech; safety/security; defamation; enforcement of court order; and other’. The posts published by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 did not contain any defamatory statements or allegations against RSS, as it was purely factual reporting based on information relating to the notice received by the Organisations on 29 October 2026.

Furthermore, criminal defamation is a non-cognizable offence which requires a court order for the police to initiate action. The Delhi Police is not empowered to issue a content takedown order for such offence via the Sahyog Portal in the absence of such an order. While the notice mentions enforcement of a court order as one of the grounds, no such court order is cited or made available in the notice. Additionally, the notice does not identify a legal basis or statutory provision for the offences of hate speech or safety/security. The notice also relies on Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and states that action must be taken by X within 3 hours.

Therefore, in light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 condemns the takedown request issued by the Delhi Police and maintains that they are unlawful, disproportionate and violative of the fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police and the concerned authorities to immediately withdraw these requests. If there exists any relevant court order directing the removal of the content, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the Delhi Police to provide copies of said order to the Organisations (https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2, IFF, and @geoblockedindia) posthaste. 

We stand in solidarity with all individuals and organisations affected by these takedown requests and reaffirm our commitment to defending their right to speak, document and question restrictions on online expression. Transparency, accountability and access to remedies must remain central to any process that seeks to restrict online expression.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. What has happened

It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. PUBLIC STATEMENT BY PARANJOY GUHA THAKURTA
On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".
My website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy does not sell financial products, solicit funds for commercial schemes, or engage in any activity that could remotely be classified as a scam. It is a repository of public-interest journalism, books, documentary films, and investigative reports built over a lifetime of work. By acting on a fabricated "Fraud/Scam" abuse report without a single verification check or prior notice to the domain owner, Hostinger has allowed its abuse-reporting mechanism to be weaponised to censor an independent journalist.
Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.
I demand immediate answers and accountability from Hostinger:
1. Who submitted the false "Fraud/Scam" abuse report against https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, and on what exact date and time was it received?
2. What internal verification did Hostinger's abuse team conduct before classifying a 12-year-old journalism portal as a "Fraud/Scam" site, especially when 92 security vendors on VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing show zero malicious or unsafe content?
3. Why was no prior notice, warning, or copy of the complaint sent to me before suspending the entire hosting account?
4. On what basis did Hostinger's specialist declare that the suspension of an entire archive of journalistic work is "not negotiable"?
While my legal advisers are in the process of taking appropriate steps in court regarding the ex parte order dated October 24, 2026, and the wholesale suspension of my website, this backdoor censorship through web hosting providers sets a dangerous precedent for the independence of the media and freedom of expression as enshrined in Article (19)(1)(a) of the Constitution of India as a fundamental right of every citizen of India.
Yours sincerely

Paranjoy Guha Thakurta
Independent Journalist, Author, Publisher and Maker of Documentary Films and Music Videos

Statement on the threats received by IFF

Over the past three days, IFF, https://t.co/eAhBlCEUwk and the operator of @geoblockedindia have received two notices said to be purpotedly issued on behalf of the RSS. As many, including us have indicated they may be fake and we have done this with humour, while also due to their plausible nature disclosing it to our community. 

The first asked us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. We replied that it was legally deficient. The second, received today, says the matter has been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints have been filed in several states, and that requests have been made to block our X accounts and suspend our organisations.

Some RSS office bearers have publicly said on X that the first notice is not authentic. We had at the time of the first notice itself written to the RSS at its official address to ask whether it authorised either. This evening, X also informed us that it has received a request from the Indian police about one of our posts. We do not yet know who made it or under what law. If it is a legal demand that results in a takedown, we will contest it.

We want to be clear about what this is. Over the past three weeks alone, IFF has assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. We have filed multiple cases for journalists, cartoonists, activists, artists, students, ordinary users. That work is the reason these notices exist as an attempt to bully and harass us. 

Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is not an offence. It is what the Constitution expects of us. We are a small team of committed constitutionalists. We will not be intimidated by threats, whoever sends them, and we will not be bullied into silence. Our work continues. We will go to court tomorrow and conduct cases, our staff will file RTIs, we will analyse tenders and challenge all forms of digital authoritarianism. We have done this work for more than a decade without fear or favour and IFF will not stop.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
Rachel Clayton: “india’s government is facing fresh questions about press freedom after dozens of journalists were detained while covering youth-led protests. reporters in the capital of new delhi fear the crackdown is part of a wider effort to control what indians see and hear. thousands came to protest, but it was those who came to report. that became the story. the committee to protect journalists says at least 43 reporters were detained while covering this month’s rallies, the vast majority in new delhi. shoaib daniyal has worked for the online newspaper scroll for over a decade.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “there was a checkpoint right outside my house. i spoke to a cop, i asked him about the protest. he became suspicious, he became angry, he said i’m going to detain you. he detained me.”

Rachel Clayton: “shoaib filmed his detention.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “why have you detained me?”

Officer: “you are wasting your time as well as mine.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “for what? what did i do?”

Rachel Clayton: “he says officers offered to release him if he wiped his phone. delete it, the officer tells him. no, he says.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “he didn’t know what to do with me, so he kind of drove me around for almost an hour and a half. eventually, i think they kind of tired themselves out and they did let me go. like, literally anyone could be just picked up and put on the bus. there seems to be no method to segregate people who may genuinely be coming in the way of police work to people who were simply there to report.”

Rachel Clayton: “police are allowed to detain anyone without a warrant under the country’s preventive detention laws, but officers must have a reasonable suspicion the person is going to commit a crime. delhi police claim they could not distinguish between traditional media and protesters filming on their phone. the latest round of demonstrations erupted over india’s election commission. protesters accused commissioner gyanesh kumar of removing millions of names from voter rolls to benefit the ruling bjp government. it comes three months after mass demonstrations forced out india’s education minister, which took everyone, including the government, by surprise.”

Former NDTV journalist: “and i think this was the response of a wounded regime, that they now wanted to hit back. they wanted to stamp out the protests using extraordinary force. and i think silencing or trying to intimidate the media in these new ways is part of that response.”

Rachel Clayton: “where do you see things pointing? he worked for ndtv for 30 years. the network won multiple awards for being india’s most trusted news brand. he resigned in 2022 when businessman gautam adani took over. the billionaire had a close relationship with the prime minister, and journalists raised concerns about editorial independence.”

Former NDTV journalist: “we’ve seen this growing pattern of the gradual takeover of media companies by corporates that are seen as close to the regime. and you also have seen separately media companies on their own flipping. so when that takeover news came, it was kind of a sign that the sort of clock had started ticking. we call them the godi media, meaning lapdog media. what is this dangerous anti-democratic ecosystem that’s being built in this country? entire swaths of particularly tv media have been brought to heel, have turned into propagandists for the government.”

Rachel Clayton: “since narendra modi took power in 2014, the majority of india’s most popular networks have been bought by corporate businesses, politicians, or people with close ties to the government. social media had begun breaking that control. ramit verma creates and publishes political satire for a large online following. he was also detained, covering recent protests. india’s government has tightened its grip on internet freedom and regularly orders social media companies to remove posts and even whole accounts.”

Ramit Verma: “it happened so much that i don’t even remember the last post that got taken down, but it’s become the norm in india right now. it’s become the norm for your posts to get taken down at any point without any explanation.”

Rachel Clayton: “this year’s wave of protests has posed one of the biggest challenges yet to prime minister narendra modi, and the detention of journalists shows the government is not afraid to use authoritarian tactics to stop the media holding those in power to account.”

Former NDTV journalist: “i wouldn’t be surprised if we’ll see a repeat of it. i think there is a kind of marked escalation now that has happened and i don’t quite know if they’re going to roll it back.”

Rachel Clayton: “a worrying sign of things to come. rachel clayton, abc news, new delhi.”

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Foreign VPNs have often been found involved in planning & execution of terror activities, funding, facilitation and radicalisation of youth and crime against children & women by spread of p€rverted content & therefore the biggest threat to the nation's security and culture. Below is my letter to GOI seeking an immediate ban on foreign VPNs & detailing instances of their blatant misuse for:

A. Terrorism and radicalisation
B. Crime against children and women
C. Financial fraud
D. Drug trafficking
E. Extortion, blackmailing, etc.

In my letter I have listed a sample of 50 serious instances of these crimes and terror activities from India and around the world.

Below is the full text of the letter :

10th November 2025

Shri Amit Shah
Union Home Minister

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw
Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology

Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal
Union Minister of State (I/C) for Law & Justice

Smt Annpurna Devi
Union Minister of Women and Child Development

Sub: Urgent Request for Immediate Nationwide Ban on Foreign VPN Services to Curb Crimes Against Children, Women, Drug Trafficking, Financial Fraud, and Threats to National Security

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

The list of crimes and terror-related incidents involving VPNs is long. We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Crimes Against Children (VPN-Enabled Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) Cases)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs (or VPN + Tor) to hide while committing Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) related crimes—downloading, sharing, or live-streaming.

1. Connecticut, USA – 2025
Michael Hull (61) used paid VPN + Tor for 4 years to access dark-web CSAM. FBI traced via VPN IP leak → DOJ
2. Minnesota, USA – Operation Grayskull, 2025
Thomas Katsampes (52) ran a 2,000-user CSAM forum requiring VPN + Tor hopping. FBI de-anonymized 18 admins via logs → DOJ
3. Florida, USA – Playpen Network, 2023–2025
956 arrests; 214 used NordVPN/PIA/Mullvad + Tor. FBI NIT malware captured real IPs on CSAM clicks → FBI
4. Germany – Boystown Takedown, 2021 (ongoing 2023 arrests)
400,000 users; rules mandated VPN + Tor. BKA arrested 72; 2 VPN providers surrendered logs under EU warrants → BKA/Europol
5. South Korea – Welcome to Video, 2019–2024
337 arrests; 41 used VPN exits in Sweden/Romania for Bitcoin CSAM buys. IRS traced VPN payments → DOJ
6. Australia – Childs Play, 2016–2017 (2023 follow-ups)
1.1M users; admin taught 3-VPN chaining + Tor. Task Force Argos caught 94 via VPN leaks → Queensland Police
7. Latin America – Operation Vibora, 2025
20 arrests; suspects used free mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder) for live-streamed child rape. VPN logs seized → Interpol
8. Oklahoma, USA – Thomas Gailus, 2025
Repeat offender used dark web via VPN to collect CSAM of prepubescents. 10-year sentence → DOJ
9. Washington, USA – Operation Restore Justice, 2025
Mitchell Dufault distributed CSAM via VPN-masked platforms. 10-year sentence → DOJ
10. Arizona, USA – 22 Defendants, 2023–2025
Multiple offenders used VPNs for CSAM possession/distribution. Charges under Project Safe Childhood → DOJ

Crimes Against Women (VPN-Enabled Cyberstalking/Sextortion)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs for cyberstalking, sextortion, or non-consensual porn against women.

1. Massachusetts, USA – James Florence Jr, 2025
Cyberstalked 13 women with paid VPNs for deepfake nudes/rape threats. 9-year sentence → DOJ
2. Albuquerque, USA – Phillip Gonzales, 2025
Sent rape-fantasy texts to 7 women via VPN-chained VoIP. VPN logs seized → DOJ
3. Global – 911 S5 Botnet, 2025
YunHe Wang sold VPN-proxied IPs for 4,000+ sextortion/rape threats against women. Servers seized → DOJ
4. Los Angeles, USA – Kody Roberts, 2023
Sent rape/murder threats to 3 women via commercial VPN. NIT grabbed IP → DOJ
5. Florida, USA – Christopher Buonocore, 2021–2024
Sextorted dozens, hired rapists via NordVPN + Tor. Bitcoin traces led to arrest → DOJ
6. Washington DC, USA – Nahvarj Mills, 2024
Posted revenge porn via Swedish VPN exits. 27-count indictment → DOJ
7. Naperville, USA – Cody Ratliff, 2025
Sextorted teen girl via mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder). Logs handed over → Police
8. California, USA – Chavarri Sextortion, 2019–2021 (2025 arrest)
Stalked/harassed women via VPN-masked accounts for nudes → DOJ
9. Global – Financial Sextortion Surge, 2023–2025
Overseas offenders used VPNs for anonymous threats; 33.5M losses → FinCEN/FBI
10. Nigeria – Operation Artemis, 2025
22 arrests for sextortion using VPNs to mask ops; 54K teen victims → FBI

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Here are 10 cases where terrorists used VPNs for propaganda, recruitment, or planning.

1. ISIS Global Propaganda – 2024
9 admins ran 150+ servers with https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM mandatory. FBI/Europol seized; logs exposed → FBI/Europol
2. Terrorgram Collective – 2024
Leaders used Mullvad + Tor for kill lists/bomb manuals. Payment slip traced → DOJ
3. Al-Qaeda Inspire Distributors – 2023–2025
14-cell used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for bomb tutorials. 3-year logs seized → Europol
4. Hamas Crypto-Fundraising – 2025
3 operatives laundered $2M via DoubleVPN Sweden exits. Logs identified wallets → DOJ
5. ISIS Sniper Channel – Minnesota, 2025
Abdelhamid Hassan uploaded 200+ videos via Safe-Inet VPN. Logs showed 18 US IPs → DOJ
6. The Base Bomb Cell – Germany/USA, 2024
5 neo-Nazis plotted via Insorg VPN C2. Logs named all → DOJ/Europol
7. Hamas Live-Stream Recruiters – Spain, 2025
9 operatives streamed via VPN-chained apps. Turbo VPN logs revealed 73 → Eurojust
8. EU Jihadist Plots – 2023–2024
24 plots (6 attacks) used VPNs for online radicalization post-Hamas Oct 7 → Europol TE-SAT
9. Al-Qaeda Online Jihad – 2023
Propaganda surge via VPN-masked uploads after Zawahiri death → Europol
10. Hamas/Al-Qassam Finance – 2025
3 campaigns dismantled; VPNs obscured cyber-finance for arms → DOJ

Other Serious Threats (VPN-Enabled Ransomware/Fraud/Etc.)

Here are 10 cases of VPN use in ransomware, hacks, fraud, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking (no overlap with prior categories).

1. ALPHV/BlackCat – US Firms, 2023
3 hackers used Mullvad/ProtonVPN for $5M ransomware. Wallet traced → DOJ
2. LockBit Hospital Attacks – TX/CA, 2024
Teen chained Nord/ExpressVPN to encrypt MRIs; 400GB leaked. Servers seized → Europol
3. $20M Real-Estate Fraud – 400 Homes, 2021–2024
Nigerian gang used IPVanish/Surfshark to divert wires. $3.2M seized → DOJ
4. Iranian Murder-for-Hire – NYC, 2024
IRGC hitmen used https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM for $100K Bitcoin scouting. Logs seized → DOJ
5. DoubleVPN – 100+ Gangs, 2019–2021
Conti/REvil used DoubleVPN for C2; 2.5K exposed via 2TB logs → Europol
6. Safe-Inet – Hive/Dharma, 2020–2025
71-country hits; Safe-Inet mandatory. BKA warrant on logs → Europol
7. Dark-Web Fentanyl Cartel – 50K Deaths, 2023–2025
Pharma-Master used VPNLab/Mullvad for 12 markets; 34 arrests → DOJ
8. DoppelPaymer Ransomware – 37 Attacks, 2023
Ukrainian core used VPNs for €10M hospital hacks (Düsseldorf). 5 arrested → Europol
9. Operation RapTor – Dark Web Drugs, 2025
288 vendors arrested; VPNs masked trafficking. €184M seized → Europol
10. MATRIX Encrypted Platform – 2024
Drug/arms/murder-for-hire via VPN-integrated comms. 2.3M messages intercepted → Europol

Foreign VPN Use in Crimes in India (2020–2025)

Here are 10 news reports from 2020–2025 detailing cases where foreign VPNs (or non-compliant international VPN services) were used to commit or facilitate crimes against children (CSAM/pornography), women (sextortion/cyberstalking), terrorism/national security threats, or other serious offenses (ransomware/fraud/drug trafficking) in India. Each includes a brief summary, crime type, and primary source link.

1. Sharp Rise in CSAM Demand via VPNs (2020)
During COVID-19 lockdown, ICPF report noted a 100% surge in child pornography searches (5M/month across 100 cities), with users employing foreign VPNs to bypass India's CSAM bans.
Crime: Child exploitation → Times of India
2. 25,000 CSAM Uploads Traced, VPNs Suspected in Access (2020)
NCMEC alerted NCRB to 25,000 child pornography uploads from India (Delhi tops list); offenders used foreign VPNs to access dark web sites, leading to FIRs and arrests in multiple states.
Crime: Child pornography distribution → The Indian Express
3. Kerala P-Hunt Operation: 47 Arrests for Dark Web CSAM (2020)
Kerala Police's covert op arrested 47 (including youth) for downloading child abuse material via foreign VPNs on darknet during lockdown; surge linked to encrypted access tools.
Crime: Child sexual abuse material → India Today
4. Porn Blackmail via VPN-Tracked Footprints (2020)
Mumbai racketeers used foreign VPNs to track porn viewers' digital footprints, then extorted bitcoins threatening exposure; cyber cell devising VPN blocks for such crimes.
Crime: Sextortion/extortion against adults (linked to child porn access) → Mumbai Mirror
5. Nagpur: 30 Arrests in 38 CSAM Cases via VPN Access (2021)
City police arrested 30 in 38 child pornography cases based on cyber intel; offenders used international VPNs to browse dark net/paid sites, prompted by NCCRP tips.
Crime: Child pornography possession → Times of India
6. Telangana: 43 Arrested for CSAM Circulation via VPNs (2023)
Cyber Crime wing arrested 43 using tip lines; suspects employed foreign VPNs to upload/share child sexual abuse material on social media/dark web.
Crime: Child pornography trafficking → The Hindu
7. Gorakhnath Temple Attack: ISIL Funding via PayPal & VPNs (2022, reported 2025)
Accused used foreign VPNs to obscure IP while transferring ₹6.7L via PayPal to ISIL supporters abroad for terror planning; FATF highlighted as national security threat.
Crime: Terrorism financing → The Hindu
8. Flight Bomb Hoax Threats via VPN-Masked IPs (2024)
Over 150 Delhi flights received hoax bomb threats on X; sender used foreign VPNs (IPs traced to London/Germany) to hide origin, complicating national security probes.
Crime: Terrorism hoax/threat to aviation security → India Today
9. Scamsters Use Rented Foreign VPNs for Ransomware/Phishing (2023)
Gujarat fraudsters rented VPNs from Marshall Islands/Australia to mask ops in ransomware, card fraud, and sextortion targeting Indians; evaded extradition via non-treaty nations.
Crime: Ransomware/financial fraud → Times of India
10. Bengaluru Rs 49Cr Fraud: Foreign Hackers Use VPN for Mule Accounts (2025)
Hackers from abroad used VPNs to breach Whizdm Finance's API, siphoning ₹49Cr via 100s of transactions; locals arrested for creating VPN-masked mule accounts.
Crime: Cyber fraud/ransomware-like theft → Times of India

Sir, the pattern is undeniable:

- Foreign VPNs openly defy Indian law.
- They enable child exploitation, pornography, violence against women, radicalization, drug trafficking and terrorist activity.

Requested Immediate Possible Actions for Consideration:

1. Publish a National Registry of Compliant VPNs
Direct CERT-In and MeitY to publish and maintain a public registry of VPN providers that have demonstrated compliance with the 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Requirement: Five-year data logging, real-time incident reporting, and appointment of an Indian-resident nodal officer.
Purpose: Establish transparency and a verifiable compliance benchmark for enforcement.

2. Delist and Prohibit Operation of Non-Compliant Foreign VPNs
Instruct Apple, Google, and all Indian ISPs to immediately delist and block all non-compliant foreign VPNs, including NordVPN, ProtonVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, and Mullvad, that have refused to adhere to the 2022 CERT-In Directions.
Action: To be taken under the blocking powers of the Information Technology Act and its associated Intermediary Guidelines.
Purpose: Prevent evasion of Indian jurisdiction and close routes for offenders hiding behind virtual foreign IPs.

3. Block Associated Payment Channels
Direct the Reserve Bank of India and all licensed payment aggregators and card networks such as PayU, Razorpay, Visa, and Mastercard to suspend or block subscription transactions to banned or non-compliant VPN providers.
Purpose: Cut off domestic funding and revenue flows sustaining illegal VPN operations.

4. Mandate Exclusive Use of CERT-In Certified VPNs
Require, through regulatory notification, that only VPNs, whether Indian or foreign, that obtain CERT-In certification be permitted to operate in India.
All VPNs advertising Indian IP services must maintain logging infrastructure within Indian jurisdiction and comply with lawful requests from enforcement agencies.
Purpose: Ensure traceability and lawful accountability of all VPN activity associated with Indian IP addresses.

5. Criminalise Intentional Use for Concealment During Offences
Propose suitable amendments or notifications under the Information Technology Act and India’s relevant penal codes to criminalise the intentional use of banned or non-compliant VPNs for concealing identity during the commission of cognisable offences involving child sexual abuse material, terrorism, radicalisation, or financial fraud.
Purpose: Target deliberate misuse while preserving lawful privacy.

6. Strengthen Traceability and Cooperation
Mandate that every VPN provider operating in India:
(a) Designate a resident nodal officer;
(b) Retain subscriber and metadata for five years; and
(c) Respond to law enforcement requests within seventy-two hours, as required by the CERT-In Directions of 2022.
Purpose: Guarantee swift investigatory access while preserving due process.

7. Establish a National Honeypot and Canarytoken Programme
Authorise CERT-In and the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit to deploy a nationwide honeypot and Canarytoken framework, as validated in peer-reviewed research, to trace VPN-enabled crimes involving child sexual abuse material, sextortion, ransomware, and terror financing.
Ensure judicial oversight, privacy protection, and certified chain of custody for admissibility of digital evidence.
Purpose: Build indigenous technical capability to unmask offenders using VPN anonymity.

8. Strengthen International Coordination and FATF Alignment
Direct NIA, CBI, and MHA’s Cyber Coordination Centre to:
(a) Formalise fast-track cooperation with FBI, Europol, and Interpol under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties; and
(b) Report VPN-linked money-laundering or terror-financing incidents to the Financial Action Task Force in conformity with its Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks dated 8 July 2025.
Purpose: Integrate India’s enforcement with global counter-terror and cybercrime frameworks.

9. Institute Annual CERT-In Audit and Enforcement Schedule
Require annual audits of VPN providers’ compliance and publish audit summaries for public accountability.
Providers failing to comply beyond sixty days after notice should face permanent blocking and notifications to RBI, DoT, and MeitY for coordinated enforcement.
Purpose: Ensure continuous oversight and eliminate recurring non-compliance.

10. Issue a Public Advisory and Compliance Deadline
Issue a national advisory within thirty days, notifying all VPN providers of a sixty-day compliance window.
After the deadline, non-compliant entities should face delisting, domain blocking, and payment interdiction without exception.
Purpose: Provide procedural fairness before enforcement action begins.

India must not remain a playground for foreign tools that shield sexual predators, criminals and terrorists. The Ministry of Home Affairs has already acted strictly—forcing Apple and Google to delist 6+ non-compliant VPNs in January 2025. It is time to complete the job.

Vande Mataram

Uday Mahurkar
Founder, Save Culture Save Bharat Foundation
Former Central Information Commissioner, Government of India

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in coordination with other Central Agencies has successfully secured the extradition of Sourabh Chandrakar, the promoter of the Mahadev App illegal betting syndicate, from Oman 

Chandrakar was detained by the Royal Oman Police following an Interpol Red Corner Notice issued against him. He is wanted in two CBI cases, in which chargesheets have already been filed, and one ED case, in which a prosecution complaint has been filed.

The CBI investigation revealed that the Mahadev Online Book was among India's largest alleged illegal online betting syndicates, operating through a network of franchised panels and branches across the country.

The syndicate allegedly offered illegal betting on cricket, football, card games and other events, while routing proceeds through mule bank accounts, multiple transactions and hawala channels. Investigators also found that part of the proceeds was allegedly used to pay protection money to public servants.

Following approval of the extradition request by Oman, a CBI team travelled to Muscat and escorted Chandrakar back to India. He will undergo a medical examination and be taken to Raipur after securing transit remand.

Chandrakar will be produced before the CBI Special Judge in Raipur tomorrow, the CBI said.

(Source: CBI)

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.
